16.13.9.en: St. Polycarp the Martyr * We pray to the eternal God, the true God, the living God, for the health of our rulers...

16.13.10.en: It is fitting for them to realize, as men, from whom they received their authority, that they have learned from the One who gave life itself. They are convinced that He is the only God, and on His power they depend completely...

16.13.11.en: To Him we Christians lift up our eyes and spread out our hands, for we are innocent, with our heads uncovered, for we have no need to be ashamed, and finally without anyone to urge us, for we pray from the heart and always make supplication for all our emperors. We ask for them a long life, a quiet empire, a secure dwelling, strong armies, a faithful senate, and a world at peace, and everything that this man and Caesar desires.

16.14.0.en: Tertullian "In the light of the king's countenance is life; and his favour is as a cloud of the latter rain" [15]

16.14.1.en: To please the king in the Lord makes him joyful, and his countenance gives life, as though he were raining upon a dry land. The latter rain is the rain that falls before the harvest, without which the earth does not bring forth a worthy yield.

16.14.2.en: If the pleasure of the king gives life to those subject to him, how much more the favor of the King of kings. As the psalmist says: "In thy presence is fulness of joy; at thy right hand there are pleasures for evermore" (Ps 16:11).

16.14.3.en: * Let us worship Him as the God of those who believe in His becoming man. For what profit is there in saying of Him that He is a man and not God, or what salvation do we have if we refuse to confess His humanity together with His divinity? Let us confess His presence, for He is both King and Physician. For Jesus the King, having become a Physician, girded Himself with the linen of our humanity and healed what was sick. The perfect Teacher of infants became an infant among them (Rom 2:20), that He might give wisdom to the foolish. The Bread of heaven came down to earth that He might feed the hungry!

16.14.4.en: * The following statement has come in the Gospel: "He that believeth not the Son shall not see life; but the wrath of God abideth on him" (Jn 3:36). The Father is angered when the only-begotten Son is despised. For a king is grieved by the mere insult to one of his soldiers. If a king is grieved merely because one of his soldiers is insulted, then if someone despises his only son, who can quench the wrath of the father on account of his only son?!

16.15.0.en: St. Cyril of Jerusalem "How much better is it to get wisdom than gold! and to get understanding rather to be chosen than silver!" [16].

16.15.1.en: To enjoy heavenly wisdom is better than all earthly riches. For wisdom adorns the soul and keeps the body from evil, so that the whole man may live enjoying God the Word, or the wisdom of the eternal God. Gold, on the other hand, gives the body a temporary beauty, or is used to acquire what sustains and nourishes the body; but the body will surely die and leave the gold behind, whereas wisdom accompanies man even in the life to come.

16.15.2.en: Spiritual understanding, the perception of the mysteries of God, and the knowledge of the depths of the divine commandment are better than silver.

16.15.3.en: * As gold is better than silver, so wisdom is loftier than prudence. The first concerns knowledge, and the latter the interpretation of what is hidden, so that you may interpret the dwellings of wisdom as the churches or the dwellings of the saints in heaven. But wisdom itself is Christ.

16.16.0.en: "The highway of the upright is to depart from evil:

16.16.1.en: he that keepeth his soul keepeth his way." [17].

16.16.2.en: The course of the upright, or their general way, is to walk without turning to the right or to the left; nothing can draw them away, neither self-righteousness or pride, nor lusts and pleasures.

16.16.3.en: When a person keeps himself, that is, takes care of his inner depths and is occupied with his eternal salvation, he keeps the uprightness of his way in the Lord, until he enjoys the divine embrace.

16.17.0.en: 18 Pride goeth before destruction, and an haughty spirit before a fall. 19 Better it is to be of an humble spirit with the lowly, than to divide the spoil with the proud. 20 He that handleth a matter wisely shall find good: and whoso trusteth in the LORD, happy is he.

16.17.1.en: "Pride goeth before destruction, and an haughty spirit before a fall" [18]

16.17.2.en: He who exalts himself falls. When Herod put on his royal apparel and sat upon his throne... the people shouted: "It is the voice of a god, and not of a man" (Acts 12:22). Immediately the angel of the Lord smote him, because he gave not God the glory, and he was eaten of worms and died.

16.17.3.en: * We ought not to think that a person stumbles and goes down into grief by a sudden fall; rather, he descends into a hopeless fall either by being deceived from the beginning, during his training, through a wrong start, or he slips from his good spiritual state gradually over a long period because of mental negligence, so that the errors increase little by little. For "pride goeth before destruction, and an haughty spirit before a fall" (Prov 16:18). It is like a house that does not fall suddenly all at once, but some defect occurs in the foundation over a long period, or it results from the neglect of its inhabitants for a long time, so that some seepage (or defect) occurs, and after this the fortified walls collapse gradually. For "by much slothfulness the building decayeth; and through idleness of the hands the house droppeth through" (Eccl 10:18); this is also what happens to the spirit.

16.17.4.en: Father Theodore * "Pride goeth before destruction, and an haughty spirit before a fall" (Prov 16:18).

16.17.5.en: Some people boast that they are the sons of rulers, and of their ability to bring down some priests from their priestly ranks; such people magnify themselves and boast for trifling matters that have no profit behind them, and therefore there is not the least reason for this self-exaltation of theirs... And there are those who boast that they have obtained what they call a privilege, Promotion, which enables them to strike off the heads of people: "the glory of these people is in their shame" (Phil 3:19). Others boast of their wealth, not true riches, but earthly wealth... All these things do not deserve even to be taken into consideration, and it is not fitting for us to boast of any of them.

16.17.6.en: The things that give us the right to exalt ourselves and boast are to boast that we are wise, or to boast (with discretion) that for ten years, for example, we have not approached bodily pleasures and lusts, or have not approached them since childhood; or again when we boast of bearing chains on our hands for the sake of the Lord Christ. These are things that call for boasting with justice; but even these things also, if we judge with our reason in truth, we find that it is not for us to exalt ourselves or boast of them.

16.17.7.en: The Apostle Paul had what could call him to boast because of the visions, revelations, miracles and signs, and because of the sufferings he bore for the sake of the Lord Christ, and because of the churches he established in many places of the world. In all this he had what could call him to boast, and according to the outward, visible things that call for boasting, the boasting of the Apostle Paul would have seemed natural to people; yet, since it was dangerous for him to boast, even about those things, the Father in His mercy, as He gave him those visions, also gave him, out of compassion for him, a messenger of Satan to buffet him, lest he be exalted; and for this reason Paul besought the Lord three times that it might depart from him, and God answered him: "My grace is sufficient for thee: for my strength is made perfect in weakness" (2 Cor 12:7-9).

16.17.8.en: Origen * Shall we praise hospitality? Shall we admire brotherly love, conjugal love, virginity, feeding the poor, singing psalms, keeping vigil in prayer all night long, and repentance? Do we humble the body by fasting? Do we dwell with God through prayer? Do we subject the lower element in us to the higher, that is, the dust to the spirit, as is proper if we judge rightly our nature, which is a mixture, like an alloy, of the two? Do we make life a meditation on death? Do we master our passions, remembering the loftiness of our second birth? Do we tame our proud and rebellious dispositions? Or our haughtiness that goes before a fall (Prov 16:18)... and our unrefined laughter, our uncontrolled eyes, our greedy ears, our immoderate talk, our wandering thoughts, or anything in us that the evil one can seize and use against us, so that death enters through the windows (Jer 9:21), as the Scripture says, by which windows are meant here the senses.

16.18.0.en: St. Gregory of Nazianzus "Better it is to be of an humble spirit with the lowly, than to divide the spoil with the proud" [19]

16.18.1.en: Humility of spirit grants a spirit of unity and harmony with the lowly, so the Lord declares His presence in their midst and grants them His grace. Pride, on the other hand, may bring great spoils and gains together with the proud, together with temporal honor, but a person loses his friendship with God and enslaves himself to the devil.

16.18.2.en: St. Augustine sees that the role of the believer in this life is to ascend as upon a tower whose top reaches heaven. This tower, rising from earth to heaven, needs the digging of foundations and a descent into the far depths of the earth. The higher the building rises, the more it needs the foundations to go down to greater depths. So whoever wants to build a tower whose top is in heaven needs to practice a deeper and deeper humility. Without the foundations of humility the tower of our spiritual life collapses, and instead of ascending to heaven with our humble Christ, our souls are completely shattered!

16.18.3.en: * Let us count the cost of the spiritual tower of towering height, and consider this carefully beforehand... Let us first take our faults clearly into account, so that we dig and remove the corruption and the refuse of the lusts, so that we may lay the strong foundations of simplicity and humility upon the solid ground... or rather, the foundations are laid upon the rock of the Gospel (Lk 6:48); by this the tower of the spiritual virtues rises, and is able to stand firm and rise to the heights of heaven in complete safety, unshaken.

16.19.0.en: Father Isaac "He that handleth a matter wisely shall find good: and whoso trusteth in the LORD, happy is he" [20].

16.19.1.en: A person may enjoy understanding and the ability to manage; he walks with understanding in the affairs of his temporal life, and receives good things, success, honor and esteem from others. But he who fears the Lord and trusts in Him receives the blessed, happy life, that is, we experience the earnest of the heavenly things.

16.19.2.en: * The upright person recognizes that when sorrows, tragedies or troubles come upon him, they are by the good will of God, and so he accepts them. But the one with a crooked heart looks at them with sorrow. He agrees that he is a sinner, but says that there are many worse than he who are happy.

16.19.3.en: The upright heart accepts everything that happens to it, saying: "The Lord gave, the Lord has taken; let Him do what pleases Him; blessed be the name of the Lord."

16.19.4.en: Troubles come from the Lord (by His permission). They are a punishment for the wicked and a chastening for the son. If you want to be a son, do not expect to escape sufferings, for He chastens every son whom He receives. Every son? Without exception?

16.19.5.en: Listen, the only-begotten Son alone is without sin, and yet He suffered.

16.19.6.en: He bore our weaknesses; the Head bore the members of the body in His person.

16.19.7.en: As a man He entered into His sufferings in sorrow, that you may rejoice.

16.19.8.en: He entered into bitterness that you may receive consolation. He said: "My soul is sorrowful unto death; but let not my will, but thy will be done, O Father."

16.20.0.en: 21 The wise in heart shall be called prudent: and the sweetness of the lips increaseth learning. 22 Understanding is a wellspring of life unto him that hath it: but the instruction of fools is folly. 23 The heart of the wise teacheth his mouth, and addeth learning to his lips. 24 Pleasant words are as an honeycomb, sweet to the soul, and health to the bones.

16.20.1.en: "The wise in heart shall be called prudent: and the sweetness of the lips increaseth learning" [21]

16.20.2.en: The heart among the Jews corresponds to the mind among the Greeks. So whoever is wise and balanced in his thinking enjoys the respect of others and their esteem for his personality.

16.20.3.en: But whoever mixes this wisdom and balance with the sweetness of the tongue increases in learning, meaning that he becomes able to deal with others, so he benefits from their work and experience, and they reciprocate in the same way.

16.20.4.en: * It was said of Abba John of Qolzum - because he lived for some time beside Qolzum, that is, Suez - that because of his great humility he carried the whole wilderness of Scetis on his little finger. How did he do that?

16.20.5.en: The elder answered: "In the old copies it is recorded that he carried it toward his will, for with discernment, knowledge, old age and humility he was greatly adorned with cheerfulness, and he met with joy all the brethren who came to him at any time to reveal to him their battles and thoughts. The meaning of this saying is that they obeyed his thought in all that he wished and said and commanded.

16.20.6.en: At that time Abba Macarius of Alexandria was the head of the monastery, and St. John drew all the monks of Scetis to his will by the life-giving word that came out of his mouth, as he taught and preached to all the brethren."

16.21.0.en: The Paradise of the Fathers "Understanding is a wellspring of life unto him that hath it: but the instruction of fools is folly" [22]

16.21.1.en: The spirit of understanding and discernment overflows with blessings upon the believer, as though he carries within him a spring that overflows upon him with life. His thoughts make him grow and advance. But the fool is not benefited by a good word or by chastening, for he insists on not learning.

16.21.2.en: * People are usually called "rational," though the word "rational" is misused. The rational are not those who study the sayings and writings of the wise early Fathers, but those whose souls are rational, able to distinguish between what is good and what is evil. They avoid what is evil and harmful to the soul, and wisely care for what is good and profitable for the soul and practice it with great thanksgiving to God.

16.21.3.en: These alone are truly those whom we must call "rational"...

16.21.4.en: We become worthy to be called human when we are characterized by reason (according to the previous meaning); if reason (in this sense) is not present, we do not differ from the dumb animals except in the shape of our limbs and the gift of speech.

16.21.5.en: Therefore, let the rational man know that he is immortal, hating the shameful passions which are the cause of the death of men.

16.22.0.en: St. Abba Anthony the Great "The heart of the wise teacheth his mouth, and addeth learning to his lips" [23]

16.22.1.en: The writer gives great importance to the heart (or mind), that is, to the inner man; if it becomes holy, it translates this holiness practically through his lips, so his words come forth uprightly, and he enjoys continual edification.

16.22.2.en: * When the rational person examines himself, he sees what he must do, and what is profitable for him, and what is akin to his soul and leads it to salvation, as he also sees what is foreign to the soul and leads it to destruction, and in this way he avoids what harms the soul as something foreign to it.

16.23.0.en: St. Abba Anthony the Great "Pleasant words are as an honeycomb, sweet to the soul, and health to the bones" [24]

16.23.1.en: The words of the godly person carry three characteristics.

16.23.2.en: The first is that they share the characteristic of the word of God, of which the psalmist speaks, that it is as the honeycomb (Ps 19:10).

16.23.3.en: Second, they do not stop at winning others and the growth of the spirit of love and friendship and the dispelling of the spirit of anger, but carry a special sweetness within the soul of the speaker himself.

16.23.4.en: And finally, together with their pleasantness and sweetness, they are profitable, for they heal the bones, which are the frame of man himself. It is as though words full of grace are profitable from every side, to the speaker and to the hearers, to the soul as to the body.

16.23.5.en: * You who love learning and long to listen, receive once more the holy words, and delight yourselves with the honey of wisdom, for so it is written: "Pleasant words are as an honeycomb, sweet to the soul" (Prov 16:24). For the work of the bees is very sweet, and benefits the soul of man in many ways; but the divine, saving honey makes those in whom it dwells skillful in every good work, and teaches them the ways of spiritual progress.

16.23.6.en: St. Cyril the Great * Be slow and dull toward idle talk, and wise and knowledgeable in listening to the words of the saving holy Scriptures. Let listening to worldly tales have a bitter taste in your mouths, but let the conversations of the saints be as the honeycomb.

16.23.7.en: St. Basil the Great * The sea is the Holy Scripture, which carries in it deep meanings and the secret depths of the prophets. Many rivers flow into this sea. Joyful and pure are these streams. These springs are calm and overflow with eternal life (Jn 4:14). There are also words that are delightful as the honeycomb (Prov 16:24), gentle conversations that water souls with the sweetness of the moral commandments. The streams of the Holy Scripture differ, and you know what you should drink first, then second, then last.

16.23.8.en: St. Ambrose The Roman senator Paulinus of Milan describes to us, concerning his friend St. Ambrose, bishop of Milan, that his father, who was also called Ambrose and was administering the provinces of Gaul, saw a swarm of bees entering and leaving the mouth of his little son, the infant Ambrose, as he lay in swaddling clothes with his mouth open. The father, his wife and his daughter feared for the child, but they watched the sight in astonishment. The swarm set out and rose high into the air until it disappeared completely. The father said in terror: "If this child lives, he will surely be of great importance." The senator comments, saying: [For the Lord was at work during the childhood of His servant so that the words might be fulfilled: "Pleasant words are as an honeycomb," for this swarm of bees was implanting the honeycomb for his works which came later, which bear witness to the heavenly gifts and direct the minds of the people from earthly things to heavenly things.]

16.24.0.en: 25 There is a way that seemeth right unto a man, but the end thereof are the ways of death. 26 He that laboureth laboureth for himself; for his mouth craveth it of him. 27 An ungodly man diggeth up evil: and in his lips there is as a burning fire. 28 A froward man soweth strife: and a whisperer separateth chief friends. 29 A violent man enticeth his neighbour, and leadeth him into the way that is not good. 30 He shutteth his eyes to devise froward things: moving his lips he bringeth evil to pass. 31 The hoary head is a crown of glory, if it be found in the way of righteousness.

16.24.1.en: "There is a way that seemeth right unto a man, but the end thereof are the ways of death" [25]

16.24.2.en: We have already spoken of these deceptive ways that seem straight to a person but lead him into eternal death (Prov 14:12).

16.24.3.en: Here the wise man warns us against relying on personal judgment without the counsel of God, and enjoying the experience of the godly who went before us on the way. Scripture warns us against man's reliance on his own thought, for it is said: "In those days there was no king in Israel: every man did that which was right in his own eyes" (Judg 17:6; 18:1; 21:25).

16.24.4.en: * Likewise, when the monk is eager to long for a holy priestly office, under the pretext of teaching people and love of winning souls, he (Satan) by this draws us away from humility and from strictness in our life.

16.24.5.en: Thus he presents to us all the things that stand in the way of our salvation and do not suit our work, but he hides them under a cover, or veils them with a veil of compassion and piety, so that he may easily deceive those who lack skill and care.

16.24.6.en: They counterfeit the coinage of the true king, for they show these works as full of compassion, but they were not minted by those who have the right to do so, that is, they do not agree with the mind of the fathers of the universal Church, and they do not obtain them from the public office assigned to issue them; rather, they are minted by stealth through satanic deception, and they slip them to the unskilled and the ignorant...

16.24.7.en: Although at the beginning they appear useful and necessary, afterward they begin to penetrate into the soundness of our work and weaken the whole structure of our aim in several ways. Therefore it is good that these thoughts be cut off and removed from us, as though they were a diseased member which, though it seems necessary, is harmful to us. For it is better for us to be without this member of some commandment, that is, not to carry it out, and to remain in peace and safety and enter the Kingdom of Heaven so, than to sin against all the commandments through the deception of Satan, who offers us to carry out some commandment, and by means of it deprives us of our strict order and arrangement, and so there comes to us a loss exceeding in importance any later harm, and it drives all our former striving and the whole body of our works into the burning of the fire of Gehenna (Mt 18:8).

16.24.8.en: It is said of these kinds of deception, "There is a way that seemeth right unto a man, but the end thereof are the ways of death" (Prov 16:25). And also, "He that is surety for a stranger shall smart for it..." (Prov 11:15). For Satan deceives us by taking on the appearance of holiness.

16.25.0.en: Father Moses "He that laboureth laboureth for himself; for his mouth craveth it of him" [26]

16.25.1.en: This proverb urges us to work diligently, whether in our daily work for temporal needs, or in spiritual work to satisfy the inner hunger.

16.25.2.en: The literal translation is "The soul that labors (strives) labors for itself." When a person feels hunger, his mouth urges him to work diligently, by the sweat of his brow, that he may eat and be satisfied.

16.26.0.en: "An ungodly man diggeth up evil: and in his lips there is as a burning fire" [27]

16.26.1.en: * Do not be one fought with the tongue. Let everyone bless you.

16.26.2.en: St. Anthony the Great * An elder said: The tongue is full of fire, and it defiles the whole body, so let him who loves his life have pity on his tongue. Guard your lips, O man of God, and bridle your tongue, and you will profit by all your labors, for he who keeps his tongue has many honors. Blessed is he who rules over his tongue, for his granaries (that is, his storehouses) are filled with good things.

16.26.3.en: * An elder said: If the movements of your tongue are abundant, the pure movements have been quenched in your heart; but if your tongue is silent and your heart boils with pure movements, blessed are you, for its movement by the Spirit lifts you to the calm of life. Silence your tongue that your heart may speak, and silence your heart that the Spirit may speak in it.

16.27.0.en: The Paradise of the Fathers "A froward man soweth strife: and a whisperer separateth chief friends" [28]

16.27.1.en: He has already spoken of the sweetness of the mouth of the wise man and what the words of grace offer to him and to those around him for the edification of all. Now he speaks of the words of the ungodly man, who, though he offers honeyed words, they are like a burning fire, destroying himself and those around him. The wicked man utters lies, kindles the fires of strife, and also corrupts friendships by his words.

16.27.2.en: By saying "diggeth up" he indicates that if he does not find what he can say of lies and deceptions, he takes it upon himself to dig in the earth and toils to find a terrible lie to utter. If Scripture indicates that the kingdom of the devil is under the earth, then it is as though the wicked man digs by his free will to meet always with the enemy of good, the liar, who teaches him lying and deceit, so that he bears his image as his son.

16.28.0.en: "A violent man enticeth his neighbour, and leadeth him into the way that is not good" [29]

16.28.1.en: By the violent man he means the man of violence, who finds his pleasure in the troubles of others.

16.28.2.en: * When a person deals with another out of malice, it (rebounds upon him) involuntarily. And it happens thus: whoever deprives (his brother) of something deprives himself of the same thing, even against his wish. So also whoever insults another falls under the judgment of those who are insulted. Whoever wrongs another falls under the judgment of those wronged, and those who blame others fall under the judgment of the blamed. Those who despise others fall under the judgment of the despised. And those who lie fall under the judgment of those slandered. I am not enumerating here; I say in brief that everyone who does wrong falls under the same judgment. The holy Scriptures bear witness to this when they say: "Whoso diggeth a pit shall fall therein: and he that rolleth a stone, it will return upon him" (Prov 27:26)... And it says also: "Is God unrighteous who inflicts wrath?!" (Rom 5:3).

16.29.0.en: St. Mark the Ascetic "He shutteth his eyes to devise froward things: moving his lips he bringeth evil to pass" [30]

16.29.1.en: Whoever commits sin in intention, closing his eyes to fall into wicked daydreams, or biting his lips from inner anger, practices evil.

16.29.2.en: The godly person closes his bodily eyes for a while, asking God to open his inner sight so that he may enjoy the vision of God's mysteries and glories, and he desires that all humanity share with him in this gift. But the wicked man scrutinizes his brother with his eyes and does not care about the injustice or distress he suffers, and shuts his lips like one who wants to take revenge!

16.30.0.en: "The hoary head is a crown of glory, if it be found in the way of righteousness" [31].

16.30.1.en: If gray hair has its dignity, it does not rest upon the color of the hair, nor upon the number of years, but upon the righteousness which he has lived and experienced. Old age cannot cause the righteous man to lose his vitality in righteousness, and his striving for the crowns. And as Caleb said: "And now, lo, I am this day fourscore and five years old. As yet I am as strong this day as I was in the day that Moses sent me: as my strength was then, even so is my strength now, for war, both to go out, and to come in" (Josh 14:10-11). And it was said of Moses: "And Moses was an hundred and twenty years old when he died: his eye was not dim, nor his natural force abated" (Deut 34:7).

16.30.2.en: * One day Abba Ammon went to visit (Abba Sisoes) and found him grieved over his coming from the wilderness. He said to him: Father, it is not good for you to grieve, because you have come near to the dwelling place of the brethren, for your body has become weak and you are no longer able to do those works that you want in the wilderness.

16.30.3.en: When Abba Sisoes heard these words, he looked at Abba Ammon sharply and answered him with anger, saying: What is this that you are saying to me, Abba Ammon? Was not the freedom of thoughts that I had in the wilderness sufficient to take the place of all works? And as for you also, Ammon, who understand life and the results of freedom of thought, and who are not subject to the necessity of wandering and disturbance of thought, nor are hindered by old age or weakness, tell me what can you do in the wilderness in advanced age? And even if I am not fit for the works of the body because I have become weak through my old age, I have more ability to accomplish the works of thought than I had in my early manhood.

16.31.0.en: "He that is slow to anger is better than the mighty; and he that ruleth his spirit than he that taketh a city" [32]

16.31.1.en: There is no greater strength than for a person, by the grace of God, to control his emotions, impulses and passions. Whoever rules over his anger is reckoned better than the mighty, and whoever rules over his depths and thoughts is greater than a king who governs a city.

16.31.2.en: * If you are angry, be angry with yourself, for thus you are stirred and do not sin. For whoever is angry with himself, since he is quickly stirred, ceases to be angry against others. But whoever wishes to justify his anger burns the more and quickly falls into sin. And as Solomon says: "He that controlleth his anger is better than he that taketh a city" - for anger misleads even the brave man.

16.31.3.en: St. Ambrose * The taking of cities is a small victory, for the places you conquer are outside us; the attaining of a greater victory is accomplished by patience, for a person conquers himself and subjects himself to himself when humility leads him to bear with others.

16.31.4.en: * Let the one who is not meek listen to the saying of the Holy Scripture: "He that is slow to anger is better than the mighty; and he that ruleth his spirit than he that taketh a city." (Prov 16:32). Victory over cities is of less importance, for what is subdued here is something external; but victory through meekness is a far greater act, for it is the mind that conquers and rules itself by itself when meekness compels the mind to control itself inwardly.

16.31.5.en: Let the wrathful understand what the Truth says to His elect: "In your patience possess ye your souls" (Lk 21:19). The manner of creation is truly a marvelous matter, in that the mind governs the soul, and the soul rules over the body. But the soul loses its control over the body if the mind does not rule over it. Therefore the Lord shows us that meekness is the guardian of our states and also teaches us that by meekness we can possess ourselves. And so we realize the gravity of the sin of lack of meekness (anger) when we see that by it we lose our very being (our existence).

16.32.0.en: "The lot is cast into the lap; but the whole disposing thereof is of the LORD." [33]

16.32.1.en: Perhaps he means that if a disagreement is found between two wise persons, and they cannot reach a decision, they pray and seek the will of God, then cast a lot, and the flood accepts the result of the lot.

16.32.2.en: In the division of the Promised Land the Lord spoke to Moses, saying: "Notwithstanding the land shall be divided by lot: according to the names of the tribes of their fathers they shall inherit. According to the lot shall the possession thereof be divided between many and few" (Num 26:55-56).

16.32.3.en: The lot was used to discover Achan, who disobeyed the Lord and took spoil and hid it (Josh 7:16-18), and the sailors were able to discover Jonah's disobedience to God (Jon 1:7). And in choosing a disciple in place of Judas, the disciples cast lots, and it fell upon Matthias (Acts 1:23-26).

16.32.4.en: * "The Apostle explains in (Acts 1:23-26) that if we use it (the casting of lots) with absolute faith, together with prayers, it will clearly reveal the will of God."

16.32.5.en: Origen Some see that after the descent of the Holy Spirit upon the Church there was no longer any need for the lot; rather, by prayer and fasting the men of God consult together under the guidance of His Holy Spirit to know His divine will.

16.32.6.en: Who is there to care for me but You!

16.32.7.en: * My soul blesses You for Your surpassing love.

16.32.8.en: You set me in Your image and likeness, and gave me freedom!

16.32.9.en: In the fullness of my freedom my depths cry out to You:

16.32.10.en: Take over my life and lead me.

16.32.11.en: There is none to sanctify me but Your Holy Spirit.

16.32.12.en: Nor any to justify me but You, nor any to open his arms to me but the holy Father!

16.32.13.en: O Holy Trinity, You are everything to me!

16.32.14.en: * You gave me mind and heart, but who sanctifies my scales but You.

16.32.15.en: Without You all the standards of my soul are disturbed.

16.32.16.en: Without You I cannot distinguish truth from falsehood!

16.32.17.en: Tame my soul with all its powers, and my body with all its members.

16.32.18.en: * Lead my thoughts, my intention and my conscience, so that my depths may walk in the spirit of uprightness.

16.32.19.en: And the light of truth shines within me!

16.32.20.en: * What shall I offer You? What shall I render to You for Your love?

16.32.21.en: You do not ask for sacrifices or offerings, and You have no need of praises and hymns of glory!

16.32.22.en: But in Your love You ask for my whole heart!

16.32.23.en: Take possession of me, that I may possess You, O Goodness itself!

16.32.24.en: * Break into my stony, haughty heart, that it may melt with Your love and be crushed in humility by Your grace!

16.32.25.en: May it be filled with love for You and for all humanity.

16.32.26.en: May it bear Your fear, so that it turns neither to the right nor to the left.

16.32.27.en: * Declare Your dwelling within me, so that the enemy of good may not come near me.

16.32.28.en: Indeed, may even my enemies be at peace with me!

16.32.29.en: * May my soul be satisfied by Your dwelling, so that it desires nothing but Your righteousness!

16.32.30.en: Fill me with the spirit of power, that I may carry within me the authority of the Spirit.

16.32.31.en: Every word that comes out of my mouth has its power, because You keep my mouth by Your power.

16.32.32.en: Every thought that passes through me will not dwell in me without Your command.

16.32.33.en: My heart is turned into a throne like the heavenly one.

16.32.34.en: And my words and deeds proceed in a manner worthy of Your Kingdom!

16.32.35.en: * Your dwelling in me leads my feelings, so I give honor to whom honor is due.

16.32.36.en: And I submit to the authorities with joy of heart!

16.32.38.en: But I respect every person, and esteem every gift!

16.32.39.en: I desire that the whole earth become heaven!

16.32.41.en: * My depths cry out to You:

16.32.42.en: Grant all humanity the wisdom that sits by Your throne..

16.32.43.en: Grant all understanding and enlightenment, that all may perceive the riches of Your surpassing divine providence!

16.32.44.en: * When shall I see all men filled with love?

16.32.45.en: Their mouths dripping honey, and their souls filled with sweetness and pleasantness?

16.32.46.en: They walk in You, O true Way, so that no one is deceived by the devil's crooked ways.

16.32.47.en: All work in the spirit of love.

16.32.48.en: And injustice and violence have no place, nor lying any room among us!

16.32.49.en: * Sanctify all, O Longsuffering One, that all may become kings and priests to God Your Father.

16.32.50.en: To You be glory and thanksgiving, O Maker of good things!

16.32.51.en: To You be praise, O You who care for all Your creation!
